questions.q: Why is sizing infrastructure for TODAY's load considered one of the most common infrastructure mistakes?
options: Today's load is always higher than future load for any growing system
Capacity planning is unnecessary for any AI system
Infrastructure sized for current load never has any capacity problems
Infrastructure built to exactly fit current load is already behind by the time it ships, since real systems keep growing while the infrastructure stays fixed
questions.explain: Planning for current load ignores the fact that load keeps growing -- by the time infrastructure sized for 'today' is actually deployed, real traffic has usually already moved past that number.

questions.q: In the worked example, Northbeam projects hitting its 5,000,000 requests/day capacity ceiling at month 7 given 15% month-over-month growth from 2,000,000. Why is this forecast more useful than just knowing the current traffic number (2,000,000)?
options: The current traffic number is always more important than any future projection
It gives a concrete future date to plan infrastructure work against, instead of a comfortable-sounding current number that doesn't reflect where the system is actually heading
Forecasting growth is only useful for systems that are already failing
The forecast and the current number convey exactly the same information
questions.explain: 'We're comfortable today' says nothing about the trajectory -- the forecast converts a growth rate into an actionable date, which is what capacity planning actually needs to drive decisions.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say 'lead time,' not the ceiling date itself, is the number that actually matters?
options: If the fix takes 3 months of engineering work, that work needs to start well before the ceiling date (e.g., by month 4, not month 7) -- the ceiling date alone doesn't tell you when to start
Lead time is irrelevant once a forecast has been made
The ceiling date is always wrong and should be ignored entirely
Lead time and the ceiling date are always exactly the same number
questions.explain: Knowing when you'll run out of capacity doesn't tell you when to start fixing it -- subtracting the fix's lead time from the ceiling date is what tells you the actual deadline to begin work.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff in capacity planning, according to the lesson?
options: Over-provisioning cost (paying for headroom you may not need yet) vs. under-provisioning risk (the chance of a capacity-driven outage) -- not simply 'always build more headroom'
There is no real tradeoff -- maximum headroom is always correct regardless of cost
Capacity planning has no real cost implications at all
The only consideration is minimizing short-term infrastructure spend, regardless of outage risk
questions.explain: Extra headroom has a real ongoing cost, so the actual decision weighs that cost against the business risk of a capacity-driven outage -- a judgment call, not a pure engineering calculation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a paid, customer-facing product usually justifies more conservative capacity headroom than a single internal tool?
options: Customer-facing products always have unlimited budgets for infrastructure
There is no meaningful difference in how these two cases should be planned
Internal tools can never experience capacity problems

An outage in a paid customer-facing product directly costs revenue and trust, which typically justifies paying more for headroom than an internal tool would, where brief degraded performance is more tolerable
questions.explain: The right amount of headroom depends on what an outage actually costs the business -- a revenue- and trust-affecting customer product has a different risk profile than an internal tool, which is why the same forecast can justify different capacity decisions in each case.
